title: RADIAL VERSUS FEMORAL APPROACH AS SECONDARY ACCESS IN PATIENTS UNDERGOING TRANSFEMORAL TRANSCATHETER AORTIC VALVE IMPLANTATION (TAVI)
summary:
Severe symptomatic high-gradient aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with a poor prognosis if not treated with valve replacement. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation has been shown in large randomized trials to be a safe and effective treatment option for patients with low, intermediate or high risk. The transfemoral approach for the heart valve is by far the most commonly used as it is fairly controlled to manage and the complication rate is low compared to other access routes. 
The TAVI procedure requires two arterial accesses: one with a large passage for the TAVI prosthesis via the femoral artery, and a smaller secondary access for a pigtail catheter that guides the implantation of the TAVI prosthesis into the optimal position. This secondary access is most commonly performed via a second transfemoral puncture, but is increasingly also being performed via the radial artery. 
Vascular complications are the most frequently observed complications of transfemoral TAVI and are associated with a poorer outcome of the procedure. Recent data suggest that secondary vascular access via the radial artery may contribute to the reduction of vascular complications after TAVI. In patients undergoing coronary angiography and/or percutaneous coronary intervention, radial access has become the preferred strategy due to the proven reduction in vascular complications compared to femoral access.
Recent non-randomized data suggest that the radial approach may be a safer alternative to the traditional femoral approach as a secondary arterial access in transfemoral TAVI. However, non-randomized retrospective comparisons run the risk of selection bias and underreporting of complications. Therefore, a prospective randomized study is needed to evaluate the value of radial access for secondary arterial access in patients undergoing transfemoral TAVI.

interventions.name: Radial approach for secondary arterial access
Transfemoral approach for secondary arterial access

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
I1.	Patients with aortic valve stenosis scheduled for transfemoral TAVI 
I2.	Heart team agrees on eligibility for transfemoral TAVI 
I3.    Age > 65 years 
I4.	Written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
E1.	Non accessible radial arteries as judged by the TAVI team
E2.	Non accessible femoral arteries as judged by the TAVI team
E3.	Hemodynamic instability
E4.	Cardiogenic shock
E5.	Currently participating in an investigational drug or another device study.. 
E6.	Lack of capability to give informed consent
E7.	Patient refuses TAVR
